<reason>A built the stronger comparative case by weighing acknowledged treatment risks against persistent distress and irreversible changes during delay. B legitimately challenged the limited long-term evidence, leaving A’s conclusion qualified rather than conclusive. However, B increasingly demanded lifetime predictive certainty from screening and treated continuation rates as evidence of treatment-induced persistence without establishing that inference. A answered the pressure questions directly, explained screening’s practical safeguards, and explicitly defended hormones where justified rather than retreating to blockers alone. Its central case survived; B’s principal counterarguments did not.</reason>
<best_rebuttal>A’s challenge to the “pipeline” inference was decisive. B answered with identity movement among broader adolescent populations, but A correctly explained that this comparison cannot distinguish treatment-induced persistence from selection of adolescents whose dysphoria persists.</best_rebuttal>
